recent_posts.title: Compare harnesses not models: Blitzy vs GPT-5.4 on SWE-Bench Pro
recent_posts.summary: An independent audit by Quesma examines whether Blitzy's agentic harness genuinely outperforms raw frontier models on SWE-Bench Pro. Blitzy scored 66.5% vs GPT-5.4's 57.7%, and the audit found no reward hacking. The key insight is that raw models like GPT-5.4 often produce 'almost correct' solutions but fail at the last mile — they don't actually run tests or verify their changes. Blitzy's edge comes from deep codebase documentation, spec-driven planning, and rigorous test verification before shipping. The post argues that for enterprise codebases (payments, mainframes, legacy systems), the agent harness and orchestration layer matters more than the base model itself, and that the race for enterprise-grade AI coding agents is just beginning.

recent_posts.title: Reviving a 20-year-old puzzle game Chromatron with Ghidra and AI
recent_posts.summary: A developer reverse-engineered the classic 20-year-old laser puzzle game Chromatron from WinXP and PowerPC binaries, porting it to Apple Silicon and WebAssembly using Ghidra, AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor with GPT-5.2-Codex, Opus 4.6), and Rust. The post chronicles four different approaches, comparing AI model capabilities for decompilation tasks, and shares practical lessons: newer models require less hand-holding, hallucinations are more harmful than admissions of ignorance, Rust is a better target language than C for AI-assisted decompilation, and starting over is sometimes better than iterating. The final result achieved 307,199 out of 307,200 pixels identical to the original. The author argues this 'vibe-decompiling' trend is accelerating, making game preservation and porting accessible beyond seasoned reverse engineers.

recent_posts.title: Observability challenges in Go according to real engineers in 2025
recent_posts.summary: Based on interviews with 14 Go developers across industries, observability in Go remains painful in 2025. Key challenges include manual instrumentation requiring months of effort, data overload from high-cardinality metrics, and distributed tracing gaps especially around databases and queues. Most teams use Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, and Loki/ELK stacks. Legacy OpenTracing is still widespread in large orgs, with migration to OpenTelemetry being slow. Developers want auto-instrumentation, span coverage analysis, and unified correlation of metrics/logs/traces without boilerplate. The post points to OpenTelemetry Go Compile Instrumentation as a potential solution.

recent_posts.title: Sandboxing AI-Generated Code: Why We Moved from WebR to AWS Lambda
recent_posts.summary: A case study on migrating AI-generated R code execution from WebR (WebAssembly in the browser) to AWS Lambda for a chart generation tool. The team initially chose WebR to offload security concerns to the browser, but encountered practical issues: incomplete package support, large download sizes (39–92MB), and complex data flow between frontend and backend. Switching to Lambda with Docker containers resolved dependency management, enabled version pinning, simplified the data pipeline, and improved UX. Key trade-offs covered include VPC network isolation, 30-second timeouts for runaway processes, and a counterintuitive AWS Lambda quirk where CPU scales with RAM allocation — requiring 2048MB provisioned even though only 205MB was used.

recent_posts.title: Claude Code + OpenTelemetry + Grafana: A guide to tracking usage and limits
recent_posts.summary: Claude Code has native OpenTelemetry (OTEL) support that lets you pipe usage metrics directly to Grafana Cloud without any extra services or proxies. By setting a handful of environment variables, you can stream structured logs and metrics to Grafana's free-tier OTLP endpoint, where they land in Loki. From there, LogQL queries power a starter dashboard tracking four key signals: API request volume, token consumption (input + output), per-session cost estimates, and P95/P99 latency. The setup takes about five minutes and eliminates the need for custom scripts, Docker stacks, or traffic proxies like LiteLLM.

recent_posts.title: Five ways to visualize the same dating dataset compared
recent_posts.summary: A comparison of five different visualizations of the same Stanford dating dataset (How Couples Meet and Stay Together), examining charts from an academic journal, The Economist, a Reddit user, Statista, and a YouTube video. Each approach is analyzed for clarity, aesthetics, and communication effectiveness. The post concludes with practical tips for better chart design and promotes Quesma Charts, an AI-powered tool for generating styled visualizations.

recent_posts.title: Getting started with Grafana in Docker using metrics, logs, traces, and profiling
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on guide to running Grafana locally using Docker, covering five practical examples: standalone Grafana setup, Prometheus metrics visualization, log analysis with Loki, distributed tracing with Tempo, and continuous profiling with Pyroscope. Each example uses Docker Compose with pre-configured data sources and sample data generators, requiring only Docker installed locally. A companion GitHub repository contains all example directories with READMEs and configuration files.

recent_posts.title: Building Grafana dashboards with AI, CLI and a bit of pragmatism
recent_posts.summary: A pragmatic walkthrough of automating Grafana dashboard creation using an LLM-powered CLI workflow. The approach explores a ClickHouse data source column by column, lets an AI (o4-mini) propose panels and generate SQL queries, then uses deterministic code to produce the final Grafana JSON. Key lessons include enforcing read-only, LIMIT-guarded queries for safety, avoiding LLMs for tasks simple functions handle better, and sidestepping Grafana's poorly-documented JSON formats by restricting output to time series and stat panels while generating the JSON programmatically.

recent_posts.title: Data Council 2025 recap and standout talks from future unicorns
recent_posts.summary: A recap of Data Council 2025, held at the Oakland Scottish Rite Masonic Temple, highlighting standout talks and startups. Key sessions covered DuckDB's history and DuckLake, Harvey's legal AI agent architecture, Turbopuffer's vector search on object storage, Hadley Wickham on LLMs in data science, SDF's Rust-based SQL engine, and MotherDuck's real-time SQL previews. The conference has a track record of spotlighting companies before major funding rounds — ClickHouse ($350M), Harvey ($300M), and CrunchyData ($250M acquisition) all presented there. Six AI Launchpad startups also pitched, including Quesma Charts (the author's own product). The author concludes Data Council is ideal for technical builders but less effective as a go-to-market channel.

recent_posts.title: Apache Iceberg practical limitations you should know in 2025
recent_posts.summary: Apache Iceberg is a powerful open table format enabling multi-engine data sharing, but it comes with real practical limitations in 2025. Key issues include metadata overhead and file explosion for small-scale or high-frequency writes, a fragmented ecosystem where Python/Rust/Go ports lag behind the Java reference implementation, incomplete write and delete support in popular engines like ClickHouse and DuckDB, performance penalties (2-3x slower than native formats), lack of built-in governance/security controls, and hard architectural limits around write concurrency (Adobe hit ~15 transactions/minute) and real-time ingestion. Cloud egress costs also undermine Iceberg's multi-cloud portability promise. Iceberg is best suited for large, slowly-changing datasets shared across query engines — not for OLTP, real-time observability, or small-data workloads.
